incidente.resumo: An opinion column on a CMS inspector general report about how the agency mismanaged the HealthCare.gov (Obamacare exchange) contracts, which experienced significant cost overruns. The author argues the contracts went wrong because the task was too large and under-understood, gaps in the legislation created an unworkable management structure, and federal contracting rules favor preventing corruption over delivering systems on time and budget. The text does not describe how the problems were resolved.

descricao.texto: The CMS inspector general report covers how the agency mismanaged the exchange contracts so that they experienced significant cost overruns; the author argues the contracts went wrong because the task was too large and the law's architects did not understand how big it was, the holes in the legislation created an impossible management structure, and the federal contracting system was optimized to prevent corruption rather than deliver working systems on time and on budget.
trechos: Or rather, one thing that went wrong: how the agency mismanaged the contracts so that they experienced significant cost overruns.
They went wrong because they could not do anything else: The task was too large, and the law’s architects didn’t understand how big it was.
The holes in the legislation created an impossible management structure.
And the federal contracting system was optimized to prevent corruption rather than deliver working systems on time and on budget.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The specified site had to do real-time verification of identities and subsidies, price search and payments to insurers, be built in three years, and work on Day One in every state that declined to build its own exchange; a request from within CMS to scale things back was refused.
trechos: They specified a site that would do real-time verification of identities and subsidies, price search, and handle payments to insurers.

This system had to be built in three years, and moreover, it could not be built the way Silicon Valley would do it: start small, roll something out, see what works and what doesn’t, then iterate, experiment, and scale until you finally arrive at the site you wanted to build.
No, this site had to work on Day One, in every state in the nation that declined to build its own exchange.

Even when a manager in CMS tried to get the administration to scale things back, officials refused, and apparently simply failed to consider the possibility that trying to do too much would mean they ended up with nothing at all.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The law provided no money to build the federal exchanges and no adequate time for open bidding, so an expedited bidding process restricted to firms already under contract to CMS was used and project management was fragmented, with policy run from one place and technology from another, leaving only a handful of bidding contractors.
trechos: There were also big holes in the mandating bill itself -- for example, there wasn't actually any money to build the federal exchanges, or adequate time to put the contract out for open bid under the usual process.

To get around these problems, and Republican opposition, they used an expedited bidding process restricted to firms already under contract to CMS, and fragmented the management of the project, running policy out of one place, technology out of another.

That meant they had only a handful of contractors bidding, and the worst sort of management structure to manage them: the sort that almost guarantees the ideas folks will generate wish lists that the implementation people can’t deliver in the time and budget specified.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Deliverables were not delivered or were delivered late, and contractors did not seem to know whom to update until well after work had started.
trechos: Deliverables were not delivered, or were delivered after deadline, and the contractors don’t even seem to have known who to update about all of this until well after the work had started.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: On one contract, CMS staff not authorized to modify it added budget-blowing work before spending was authorized, and contract staff do not seem to have noticed because the contractor reported only billings in its monthly report, not forecasted total cost.
trechos: For example, on one contract folks at CMS who were not authorized to modify the contract added budget-blowing work before they got authorization to spend the extra money, and the contract folks don’t even seem to have realized this was happening, because the contractor was only reporting billings in its monthly report, not forecasted total cost.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: According to the author, the federal contracting system is slow and unwieldy by design, which does not suit a three-year deadline for a complicated technology project.
trechos: The federal contracting system is of course also incredibly slow and unwieldy.

But if you have a three-year deadline to deliver a complicated technology project, then a system that slows everything down, while encouraging clock-punching, is really not the system you would expect to produce it.

acoes.texto: Recommendation to CMS (from the inspector general report, as described in the column): the agency should have managed the contract paperwork better.
trechos: The inspector faults CMS for this, and thinks the agency should have managed the paperwork better.

observacoes: This is a third-party opinion column; the stated causes are the author's interpretation, and the author considers the inspector general's paperwork and disclosure findings 'side issues'. The only prevention-like content is the inspector general's view, as reported, that CMS should have managed paperwork better; it is not a commitment by the agency. The title is repeated and the text ends with an editor contact line. causa_raiz is vaga because the causes are organizational, with no technical mechanism.
